parole.testo: Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish آرناود (Arnavut).

parole.significato: honorific address on an adult male; mister, sir, efendi
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish افندی, from Byzantine Greek ἀφέντης (aphéntēs), from Ancient Greek αὐθέντης (authéntēs), from αὐτο- (auto-) + *ἕντης (*héntēs) + -της (-tēs).
From Ottoman Turkish یڭیچری (yeñiçeri).
From Ottoman Turkish پابوج (pabuc), from Persian پاپوش (pâ-puš).
Garrison-language, borrowed from Ottoman Turkish باصقینجی ار (baskıncı er, literally “man who does a باصقین (baskın, “raid”)”).
From Ottoman Turkish پاشا (paşa).

parole.significato: ban, a title in the Southeastern Europe
parole.testo: From Ottoman Turkish بان (ban), from Proto-Slavic *banъ.

Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish پورتقال (portokal), or more likely from Greek πορτοκάλι (portokáli). Doublet of الْبُرْتُغَال (al-burtuḡāl, “Portugal”), taken directly from the Portuguese or through a Romance cognate.

parole.significato: bashraf, an instrumental music form in Arabic music
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish پیشرو (peşrev, “forerunner; prelude, overture”), the first part being Persian پیش (piš, “fore-”), the latter part رو (rav) used in formed words meaning “something that goes”.
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish پیشكیر, from Classical Persian پیشگیر (pēšgīr).

Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish باصمه (basma, “printed, something pressed”). Analyzed as an instance noun (on the pattern of such words as رَسْمَة (rasma, “a drawing; an artwork”) and بَسْمَة (basma, “a smile”)), forming the denominal root ب ص م (b ṣ m).
From Ottoman Turkish پاتاتس (patates), from Greek πατάτες (patátes), from Spanish patata, from Taíno batata.
From Ottoman Turkish بكسمات (peksimet), بكسماد (beksemad), from Greek παξιμάδι (paximádi, “twice-baked piece of bread”).
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish باقلوا (baklava).
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish باقراج (bakrac).
From Ottoman Turkish بالطه (balta).
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish بلوك (bölük).
From Ottoman Turkish پانجار (pancar, “beetroot”), from Armenian բանջար (banǰar, “edible greens, vegetable”), from Old Armenian բանջար (banǰar, “edible greens, vegetable”).

parole.significato: boza, or a beverage produced by fermentation
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish بوزه (boza).
Likely derived from Ottoman Turkish بوز (buz, “ice”).
From Ottoman Turkish بوغاز (boğaz).
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish بیراق (bayrak).

parole.significato: bey, beg; a title used in the Ottoman Empire
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish بك (beg) (modern Turkish bey).
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish ترزی (terzi), from Persian درزی (darzi), from Middle Persian dlcyk' (darzīg). whence also دَرْزِيّ (darziyy).
From Ottoman Turkish ترسانه (tersane), from Ligurian tersaná, from Arabic دَار الصِّنَاعَة (dār aṣ-ṣināʕa, “industry house”).
From Ottoman Turkish طاتلو (tatlı). Doublet of دَاطْلِيّ (dāṭliyy, “a syrup-wallowed pastry”).

parole.significato: Sufi lodge, used for praying and other religious ceremonies, also used as a hostel for wanderers; takya
parole.testo: From Ottoman Turkish تَكیه (tekye), from Classical Persian تَکْیَه (takya), Arabicized as if it were from root ت ك ي (t k y) using the pattern فَعِيلَة (faʕīla) with plural فَعَالَى (faʕālā) (like هَدِيَّة (hadiyya), plural هَدَايَا (hadāyā)).
From Ottoman Turkish توج (tuc, tuç).
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish تیزه (teyze).
From Ottoman Turkish تیمار (timar), from Middle Persian [script needed] (tymʾl /⁠tēmār⁠/).

parole.significato: gage, Prunus domestica subsp. italica (fruit and tree)
parole.testo: From Ottoman Turkish جان اریكی (can eriği).
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish چاودار (çavdar).

parole.significato: where one places ammunition or artillery, powder magazine
parole.testo: From Ottoman Turkish جبخانه (cebhane, cephane).
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish گَرْدَل (gerdel).
From Egyptian dialects, borrowed from Ottoman Turkish چفت (çift).

parole.significato: sack, such as to store grain or potatoes
parole.testo: From Ottoman Turkish چوال (çuval, “sack”), from Persian گوال (govâl, “sack”).
From Ottoman Turkish چوقه (çuqa, çuha).

Not a classical word. Given that the natural distribution of Angelica archangelica and other Old World species has its southern limit not much beyond the Caucasus and Central Asia, probably a calque of Ottoman Turkish ملك اوتی (melek otu, “angelica”) and that of French angélique – Meninski yet does
From Ottoman Turkish خدیو (ḫediv, ḫıdiv), from Persian خدیو (xadêw, xedêw, “lord, master, king”).

parole.significato: a kind of pastry made of a batter fried gold-brown and wallowed when still hot in syrup
parole.testo: From Ottoman Turkish طاتلو (datlı, “sweet”) in the pastry’s name طولومبه طاتلیسی (tulumba datlısı, tulumba tatlısı). Doublet of تَطْلِيّ (taṭliyy, “jam”).
Ottoman Turkish دشمه (deşme, “an opening or a thing dug into”), the resultative noun from Ottoman Turkish دشمك (deşmek, “to cleave, to puncture”), from Proto-Turkic *teĺ- (“to make holes”).
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish تمغا (damga, “stamp”).
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish طوڭدرمه (dondurma).

parole.significato: the state of an instrument being correctly tuned
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish دوزن (düzen).
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish دومن (dümen, “helm, rudder”).
From Ottoman Turkish دونوم (dönüm) belonging to دونمك (dönmek, “to turn”), presumably a calque from Byzantine Greek στρέμμα (strémma, “stremma”, literally “that which is turned”).

parole.significato: Dönmeh, a group of Sabbatean crypto-Jews
parole.testo: From Ottoman Turkish دونمه (Dönme).
From Ottoman Turkish زنبرك (zemberek).
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish صوجوق (sucuk).
From Ottoman Turkish سر (ser), from Persian سر (sar).
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish سمیت / سمید (simit), from Persian سمید (semid, “semolina”), from Arabic سَمِيد (samīd, “semolina”).

parole.significato: a type of local administrative division, sanjak, district
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish سنجاق (sancak).
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish صڭسار (sañsar).
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish سونكو (süngü, “bayonet”).
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish چویرمه (çevirme, “spinning, rotating”).
A reborrowing from Ottoman Turkish چوراب (çorap), doublet of جِراب (jirāb).
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish چارشاف (çârşaf), from چادر شب (çâdır-ı şeb), from Persian چادر شب (čâdar-e šab).
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish چركس (çerkes).

parole.significato: a jewelled aigrette worn on the head as a military decoration
parole.testo: From Ottoman Turkish چلنك (çelenk).
From Ottoman Turkish شماندوره (şamandura).
From Ottoman Turkish شنلك (şenlik).

parole.significato: hook (a crooked device applied into things)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish چنگال , چنگل (çengel, “hook”), from Persian چنگال (čangâl).
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish ساج (sac, “frying surface”).

parole.significato: the piece of metal called nut
parole.testo: From Ottoman Turkish صومون (somun, “loaf; nut”), perhaps secondarily aligned to the root ص م ل (ṣ m l) related to firmness.
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish طبان (taban, “sole”).
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish طابور (tabur, “battalion”) and extended in sense.
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish تارم (tarim) and Persian تارم (târem) and ultimately Mongolic, see the Persian entry.
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish تازه (tâze). Doublet of طَازَج (ṭāzaj) from Middle Persian.

parole.significato: staff, crew, team, personnel (human resources working together occupying a facility)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish طاقم (takım, “group, crew, set”). Variant: طَقْم (ṭaqm, “arranged set, suit”).
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish طبانجه (tabanca, “pistol”), from طبان (taban, “sole of a foot”) + ـجه (-ca).

parole.significato: pickle, vegetable made to last with vinegar or salt
parole.testo: From Ottoman Turkish ترشی (turşı, turşu).
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish طاقیم (takım, “group, crew, set”). Variant: طَاقِم (ṭāqim, “staff, crew”).
From Ottoman Turkish طولومبه (tulumba), from Italian tromba. Doublet of طُرُمْبَة (ṭurumba) directly borrowed from Italian.

From Ottoman Turkish تاوه , طاوه (tava, “frying pan”), from Classical Persian تاوه (tāva), from Middle Persian tʾp̄k' (tābag), whence also طَابَق (ṭābaq). parole.significato: toshka, a grilled sandwich of spiced meat with conjoint fillings similar or in edge cases identical to shawarma, dürüm,…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish دوشك (döşek, “bed, mattress”) + ـَة (-a).
From Ottoman Turkish توغ (tuğ) and earlier Turkic languages.

parole.significato: elegance, grace, vigor; haughtiness, levity in character
parole.testo: From طَارَ (ṭāra, “to fly”). Seemingly as the word for an airplane coined first in Ottoman Turkish طیاره (tayyare) around 1910.
Reborrowed from Ottoman Turkish عرضحال (arzıhal, arzuhal), from Persian عرضحال, from Arabic عَرْض (ʕarḍ) + حَال (ḥāl).
From Ottoman Turkish اردو (ordu).

parole.significato: estate, manor, housing of rural workers
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish ایزبه (izbe).
From Ottoman Turkish آفرین (aferin).

parole.significato: sandie (a kind of sablé biscuits with nuts and/or raisins)
parole.testo: A vernacular borrowing of Ottoman Turkish قرابیه (kurabiye), غرابیه (gurabiye, “an almond-biscuit; a small hunting-case watch”), a pseudo-Arabism like جمهوریت (cumhuriyet) suffixed ـیت (-iyyet) from Arabic غُرَاب (ḡurāb, “the extremity of the haunch, bend of the scabbard”) because the fob watch was

parole.significato: bean, French bean (various Phaseolus vulgaris types of preparations and plants)
parole.testo: From Ottoman Turkish فاصولیه / فصولیه (fasulye, fasulya), from Greek φασούλια (fasoúlia), φασολιά (fasoliá). See South Levantine Arabic فاصوليا (faṣūlya).
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish فرچه (fırça), فورچه (furça), from Byzantine Greek βρούτζα (broútza), from Vulgar Latin *bruscia, a Germanic borrowing, equalling German Bürste.

parole.significato: a kind of traditional vest with gold braid ornaments resembling a صَدْرِيَّة (ṣadriyya), kirtle, gilet, plastron
parole.testo: Introduced in the 18ᵗʰ century after Turkish cuts, dissimilated from Ottoman Turkish فرمنه (fermene, “a kind of ornamented jacket worn in front of the waist”), from the term surfacing in Arabic as فَرْمَان (farmān, “a written decree”), understood as lending dignity carried in front for passthrough.
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish فشك (fişek, “cartridge”).

parole.significato: a dish of minced mutton or beef
parole.testo: From Ottoman Turkish قاورمه (kavurma).

parole.significato: a kind of cylindrical hat or قَلَنْسُوَة (qalansuwa) made of felt
parole.testo: From Ottoman Turkish قاوق (kavuk, “a wadded or bulbous cap; a hollow thing, a bladder”).

parole.significato: cantaloupe (Cucumis melo var. cantalupo and its fruit)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish قاون (kavun, “melon”), from Proto-Turkic *kagun.

parole.significato: strap or belt of leather or the like
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish قایش (kayış).

parole.significato: bruiser, leg-breaker, bully boy, thug, rowdy
parole.testo: From the Ottoman Turkish predecessor of Turkish kabadayı (“rowdy”). Associated by folk etymology with قَبَضَ (qabaḍa, “grab, grasp”), قَبْضَة (qabḍa, “fist”).

parole.significato: qirsh; a currency denomination used in the Ottoman Empire
parole.testo: Back-formation from the plural, itself borrowed from Ottoman Turkish قروش (modern Turkish kuruş), from German Groschen.

From Ottoman Turkish قازمه (kazma, “pickaxe”), from Ottoman Turkish قازمق (kazmak, “to dig out, to excavate”), ultimately from Proto-Turkic *kaŕ- (“to dig out”). From the common cross-cultural depictions of dwarves working the earth, likely bolstered by the real-life use of smaller individuals in mi
From Ottoman Turkish قاشقوال (kaşkaval), from Italian caciocavallo.

Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish قیشله (kışla, “barracks”). The sense of a hospital derives as a euphemism employed by soldiers. All senses are outdated in literary use and belong to the 19ᵗʰ century but this word is still used in names of specific objects.
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish قیصاج (kısaç).

parole.significato: screw, bolt, a threaded metal fastener
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish قلاغوز (kılavuz), meaning a “guide”, also in the mechanical sense.
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish خمبره (humbara, kumbara, “an earthenware box, a small jar; a bombshell”), from Persian خمباره (xombâra, “an earthenware box, a small jar; a bombshell”).

parole.significato: a kind of sailing boat of up to two masts used for housing and for pleasure-trips, for example on the Nile by sultans o…
parole.testo: Shortened from Ottoman Turkish قانجهباش (kancabaş, “ship of a curved prow”) from قانجه (kanca, “hook”) + باش (baş, “prow”), so called because of its prow being curved like a hook.

parole.significato: cloths wrapped around an infant, “baby roll”, swaddling-clothes
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish قونداق (kundak, “bundle, faggot; rifle butt”), from Byzantine Greek κοντάκιον (kontákion), diminutive of Byzantine Greek κόνταξ (kóntax, “pole”), diminutive of κοντός (kontós, “pole”).

From Ottoman Turkish قوندوز (kunduz), ultimately from Proto-Turkic *kunduŕ; cognates with Turkish kunduz, Azerbaijani qunduz, Kazakh құндыз (qundız), Bashkir ҡондоҙ (qondoð), Chuvash хӑнтӑр (hănt̬ăr), Southern Altai кумдус (kumdus).
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish قهوهجی (ḳahveci).

parole.significato: archer, he who is equipped with a bow
parole.testo: Occupational noun of قَوْس (qaws, “bow”). The sense of a consular guard is a semantic loan from Ottoman Turkish قواس (kavvas).

parole.significato: crupper (thong to keep the saddle from sliding forth)
parole.testo: From Ottoman Turkish قوش (kuş, “the rump or hock of a horse”).

Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish کتابخانه (kitabhane), borrowed from Classical Persian کِتَابْخَانَه (kitābxāna), from کتاب (ketâb) + خانه (xâne, “house”). By surface analysis, كِتَاب (kitāb) + خَانَة (ḵāna).

parole.significato: the governor's secretary or his deputy
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish كتخدا, from Persian کدخدا.
From Ottoman Turkish قرباچ (kırbaç).

parole.significato: A sort of hard, plum-sized cookie, normally made with semolina and nuts
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish كرپیچ (kerpiç, “unbaked brick”) comparing the raw states of bricks and this pastry, in the form كَرْبِيج (karbīj), then using كَرَابِيج (karābīj) as a plurale tantum, then back-forming كَرْبُوجَة (karbūja), كَرْبُوج (karbūj).
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish كارخانه (kârhane).

parole.significato: a robe of fur, a stuffed mantle, a pelt ferace
parole.testo: From Ottoman Turkish كورك (kürk, “fur”).
From Ottoman Turkish قرانتینه (karantina), from Italian quarantina.
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish كوشك (köşk).
From Ottoman Turkish كلیم (kilim), from Persian گلیم (gelim), from Ancient Greek κάλυμμα (kálumma, “covering”) from καλύπτω (kalúptō, “to cover”).
From Ottoman Turkish كنار (kenar), from Persian کنار (kanâr).
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish كوپری (köpri).
From Ottoman Turkish كورك (kürek, “shovel”).

parole.significato: a double-point win in backgammon, achieved by clearing all pieces before the opponent has begun clearing theirs
parole.testo: From Ottoman Turkish مارس (mârs), from Italian marcia or marcio.
From Ottoman Turkish مجار (macar), from Hungarian magyar.
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish مدنیت (medeniyyet), itself ultimately coined from Arabic elements. Relative noun (nisba) composed of مَدَنِيّ (madaniyy) + ـِيَّة (-iyya).
From Ottoman Turkish مزه (meze), from Persian مزه (maze, “taste, snack”).

parole.significato: printery, printing press, print shop, any place that prints
parole.testo: From Ottoman Turkish مطبعه (matbaʾa), a noun of place from the root ط ب ع (ṭ b ʕ). Printing did not start in the Arab world until Napoléon brought a printing press to Egypt in 1798, whereas the Ottomans had first private tries from 1726 (it did not become widescale until the next century).

Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish مغازه (mağâza), borrowed from Byzantine Greek μαγαζίον (magazíon), borrowed from Venetan magazén, borrowed from Arabic مَخَازِن (maḵāzin), from مَخْزَن (maḵzan), from خَزَنَ (ḵazana).
Verbal noun of the verb نَابَ (nāba, “to afflict, to occur”). The sense of a troupe of musicians is probably a semantic loan from Ottoman Turkish نوبت (nevbet, nöbet).
From Ottoman Turkish خانم (hanım).
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish اوجاق (ocak, “hearth”).
